cards.name: Nonfiction book proposal
cards.summary: The business case that sells an unwritten nonfiction book to an agent or editor: what the book is, who buys it, why this author, which recent books prove the market, and enough sample writing to show the author can deliver. A good one reads like an investment memo with a writer's voice, not like a diary of the idea.
use_for: selling a nonfiction book (business, self-help, memoir-with-a-lesson, history, popular science) before it is written
approaching Indian or international literary agents and trade publishers' nonfiction editors
a ghostwriter's first paid deliverable before the full book contract
testing whether an idea is a book or only an article
avoid: fiction and most children's books: they sell on a finished manuscript plus a query letter (genre:query_letter, genre:synopsis)
a proposal that is mostly the author's life story: lead with the reader's problem and the book's promise, put biography in the platform section
self-publishing on KDP: you need a book description and keywords (genre:kdp_book_description), not a proposal

literary agents polishing a client's pitch
ghostwriting clients as the first phase of a book deal
cards.value_why: Reedsy runs proposals as their own ghostwriting service with a published guide band of $750-$10,000 (2026); the EFA 2026 chart prices proposal development under Other Consulting at $87.50-135.00 per hour.
cards.goal: The agent or editor asks for the full proposal or a call, then offers representation or a contract.

structure.does: Opens with the reader's problem or a striking scene, states the book's promise in one sentence, the title and subtitle, the angle no other book takes, and the format (word count, delivery date).
Names a reachable reader (e.g. 'first-generation founders running Rs 1-20 crore family businesses'), not 'everyone'; says where they already buy and read.
Lists recent, real books the same reader bought, each with author, publisher and year and one line on how this book differs. Shows a market exists and is not saturated.
Why this author: credentials, first-hand experience, and audience with numbers (newsletter subscribers, followers, talks per year, media). Platform often decides nonfiction deals.
What the author will actually do: named events, partnerships, bulk-buy contacts, owned channels, dated commitments. Only things the author controls.
Every chapter with a working title and a paragraph that states what the reader learns and the story or evidence that carries it.
One or two finished chapters (usually the introduction plus one strong chapter) that prove the voice and the promise.

length.note: Sample chapters are most of the length; the proposal body without them is usually far shorter. Follow the agent's or publisher's submission guidelines when they set a format.

checklist: Can the book's promise be read in one sentence in the first 150 words of the overview?
Is the target reader a group you could find and count, not 'anyone interested in X'?
Is every comparable title a real book with author, publisher and year (none invented, none older than the market it proves)?
Does each comp line say how this book differs, not only that it is similar?
Does the platform section give audience numbers with their channel, not adjectives like 'large following'?
Is every marketing promise something the author will do personally, with a date or quantity?
Does every chapter summary say what the reader gets, not only the topic?
Does the sample chapter deliver on the promise made in the overview, in the same voice?
pitfalls: Inventing comparable titles or sales figures: the agent checks. If you cannot verify a comp, leave '[COMP: verify title, publisher, year]' for the client.
Claiming 'there is no book like this': it reads as either no market or no research. Show 2-3 neighbours and the gap between them.
Marketing plans full of things the publisher does ('get reviews in major papers'). Replace with the author's own channels and contacts.
Chapter outlines that list topics ('Chapter 4: Leadership'). Write the argument and the story for each chapter.
Overselling ('this book will change the world'). Make one specific, believable promise and back it with the author's evidence.
cards.exemplar_brief: Overview, target readership and comparable-titles sections of a proposal for 'The Kirana Playbook', a practical book on modernising neighbourhood grocery stores by an Indore retail consultant who has advised 140 kirana owners and has 38,000 LinkedIn followers; pitched to an Indian literary agent for trade publishers; English (Indian English); 900-1,400 words; mark any comp you cannot verify as [COMP: verify].

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C2. Opens on a real counter scene (udhaar register, unanswered order phones, dead stock since Diwali), one-sentence promise lands at about word 130, title/subtitle, counter-level angle and format all present; readership is three countable groups with where they buy; 140 owners and 38,000 LinkedIn followers used. Comps are real and correctly cited (E-Myth Revisited, HarperBusiness 1995; Profit First, Portfolio 2017; Jugaad Innovation, Jossey-Bass 2012), each with a difference line, and the recent Indian comp is an honest [COMP: verify] slot. Writer faults: the 1995 comp breaks the card's 'none older than the market it proves' check (the text even admits it), and two meta lines echo the card ('That is the promise of the book in one sentence...', 'The angle no other book takes is...'); cut them before it goes to an agent.

cards.name: Book summary content
cards.summary: An article, carousel or video script that condenses one book's key ideas into takeaways for people who will not read the whole book. Good ones paraphrase in the writer's own words, add an applied example for the reader's life, and say who should read the full book; they do not reproduce the book.
use_for: blog posts and newsletters ('5 ideas from X that changed how I run my shop')
Instagram or LinkedIn carousels summarising a book
YouTube or reel scripts in a 'book in 10 minutes' format
affiliate pages that end with a link to buy the book
avoid: copying passages, chapter structure or long quotes: summarise in your own words and keep quotes short and attributed
summarising a book you have not read or checked: AI-generated summaries invent chapters and quotes, verify against the book
a full critical evaluation for a literary audience: use genre:critical_review

sources.title: Fiverr: Book & eBook Writing category
sources.supports: Book & eBook writing is a Fiverr subcategory; book summary appears as a listed inclusion (774 gigs on 2026-10-04, per harvest)

buyers: creator pages and newsletters in self-improvement, business and finance
corporate L&D teams wanting book notes for staff
cards.value_why: Fiverr lists book summary only as an inclusion inside Book & eBook Writing (774 gigs, 2026-10-04); it is a volume, low-rate job unless tied to a creator's own audience.
cards.goal: The reader can state and apply the book's main ideas, and decides whether to read or buy the full book.

structure.part: Hook and who it is for
structure.does: Names the reader's problem the book solves and who will get the most from it.
Title, author and the core argument in the writer's own words.
Each idea in plain words, the book's evidence or story in one line, and one applied example set in the reader's world (a Pune office-goer, a UPSC aspirant).
structure.length: 3-7 ideas, 60-150 words each (1 slide or 20-40 seconds each)

structure.does: One honest weakness, outdated claim or context that does not fit Indian readers.
Who should read the full book, who can skip it, and the next action (read, save, buy link with disclosure).

length.note: Carousel versions sit near the bottom of the range, blog articles at 700-1,500 words, video scripts by runtime. Number of ideas drives length.

checklist: Are the book's title and author named near the start?
Is every idea written in the writer's own words, with no quote longer than one or two sentences?
Is each quote attributed and checkable against the book?
Does each key idea have an applied example for the target reader, not just a restatement?
Is there at least one limitation or critique?
Does the piece say who should read the full book and who can skip it?
If there is an affiliate link or free copy, is that disclosed?
pitfalls: Hallucinated content: an idea, chapter or quote the book does not contain. Check each idea against the book or a reliable index before publishing.
Ten ideas, each one line long: the reader remembers none. Pick the 3-7 that matter and give each an example.
Pure praise. One honest limit makes the rest believable.
Long quotation to fill space: this is the copyright risk. Paraphrase and keep quotes short.

ban.label: long quotation from the book (paraphrase instead)

cards.exemplar_brief: Blog article summarising Cal Newport's 'Deep Work' for an Indian edtech blog read by UPSC and CA aspirants studying at home; 5 key ideas, each with an example from a 10-hour study day in a shared flat; one critique; verdict on who should read the full book; English; 800-1,100 words; CTA: save the article and try one idea this week.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Hook is the reader's own 10-hour day; title, author, publisher and year up front; core argument in one line; five ideas that are faithful to the book (attention residue, rhythmic philosophy, breaks from focus, craftsman tool test with the 30-day quit, time-blocking and 'Shutdown complete') each with a concrete shared-flat study-day application; a fair critique (written for people with doors and money for grand gestures, anecdote over data); read/skip verdict and the briefed CTA with one first step. 997 words, no long quotes.

cards.name: Brand manifesto
cards.summary: A short, rousing statement of what a brand believes, what it is against and what it promises, written to be read aloud: in a launch film, on a wall, on the About page. A good manifesto could only belong to this brand and makes its own customers want to repeat it.
use_for: launch or relaunch films (voice-over script)
About page and packaging inserts
internal culture documents and onboarding
a rallying text before a tagline is chosen
avoid: product announcements or offers: a manifesto sells a belief, use genre:landing_page or genre:social_ad_copy for the offer
brands with no real point of view or proof: write genre:brand_story or genre:mission_vision_values first
lines any competitor could sign ('we believe in quality'): run the swap test below

sources.title: ProCopywriters: How to write an effective brand manifesto
sources.supports: UK copywriters' association guide treating the manifesto as a commissioned piece

sources.title: Jansen Communications: Brand messaging services
sources.supports: brand messaging packages list manifesto alongside tagline, value proposition, mission and tone of voice

sources.title: Wikipedia: Think different (Apple, 1997)
sources.supports: the campaign whose 'Here's to the crazy ones' text is the most cited manifesto example; study it, do not copy it

sources.title: Upwork In-Demand Skills 2026 (2026-02-04)
sources.supports: top-10 most in-demand Sales & Marketing skills include Email Marketing, Marketing Automation, Lead Generation; fastest-growing include Brand Strategy (+26%) and Social Media Strategy (+36%)

buyers: D2C and consumer brands at launch or rebrand
challenger brands entering a crowded category
cards.value_why: Sold inside brand-messaging packages rather than alone (Jansen); Upwork In-Demand Skills 2026 lists Brand Strategy among fastest-growing marketing skills (+26%), which carries manifesto work with it.
cards.goal: The reader feels the brand stands for something they also believe, and remembers one line of it.

structure.does: A belief or an enemy stated plainly and with tension ('Fast fashion forgot who makes your clothes.').
What is wrong in the category or the world, in concrete images the audience has seen.
A run of belief lines, often anaphora ('We believe... We believe...'), each concrete and tied to something the brand actually does.
What the brand will do and refuse to do, with at least one provable detail (a number, a process, a person).
Invites the reader in and lands on the brand name or line.

length.note: Film versions are timed to the edit (often 45-90 seconds of voice-over); wall and pack versions are cut to the strongest 4-6 lines.

checklist: Swap test: if you replace the brand with its closest competitor, does at least half the text stop being true?
Does the opening line contain a belief or an enemy, not a description of the company?
Is every belief line tied to something the brand does or makes?
Is there at least one concrete, provable detail (a number, a place, a process)?
Does it read aloud in one breath per line, without tongue-twisters?
Does it end on a line short enough to be quoted?
Are claims that sound factual (sustainable, handmade, chemical-free) true and provable?
pitfalls: Abstract virtue words (passion, excellence, innovation) with no picture behind them. Replace each with the thing the brand does: 'we pay weavers before we sell the saree'.
Copying the rhythm of a famous manifesto so closely it reads as a parody. Use the structure, not the cadence.
Green or ethical claims with no proof: in an ad these fall under the ASCI code. Keep to what the brand can show.
Too long: a manifesto that needs scrolling has become an essay. Cut to the lines that survive the read-aloud.
cards.exemplar_brief: Brand manifesto for 'Chhaap', a Jaipur hand-block-print apparel label (Sanganer printers, natural dyes) launching a slow-fashion line for urban women 25-40; used as the 60-second launch-film voice-over and the About page; English with two or three Hindi words; 120-200 words; must pass the swap test against fast-fashion brands.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C2. Opens on the enemy in images (a new collection every Friday, a bag of clothes by the door), tension, a four-line 'We believe' run each tied to the craft (the block-join shift left in, natural dye bright enough for a Monday meeting), a promise with a place and process (hand-printed in Sanganer, natural dyes, no weekly drops) and a quotable close ('Chhaap. Made to leave a mark.'). Passes the swap test against fast fashion; 171 words reads as a 60-second VO. Only nit: 'Just clothes made dheere' is the one forced Hindi insert; 'dheere-dheere' or a Hindi line in its own right would sound natural.

cards.name: Brand / business naming
cards.summary: A shortlist of names for a company, product or app, each with a rationale, pronunciation and meaning checks and flags for domain, social handle and trademark availability. Good naming work shows the territories explored and why the finalists fit the positioning; the writer flags conflicts and a lawyer clears them.
use_for: new companies, D2C brands, apps and product lines
renaming after a merger, pivot or trademark dispute
naming a sub-brand, feature, scheme or campaign
avoid: promising a name is 'available' or 'cleared': the writer runs preliminary checks, a trademark attorney clears
a single 'perfect' name: deliver a shortlist across territories so the client can choose
taglines and slogans: use genre:tagline_slogan once the name is fixed

sources.title: Fiverr: Business Names & Slogans subcategory
sources.supports: 1233 gigs on 2026-10-04; filters Company, Product, Website/App; add-ons Domain research, Trademark check, Social media handles

cards.value_why: Fiverr's Business Names & Slogans has 1,233 gigs (2026-10-04) split by company, product and app naming, with trademark, domain and handle checks as paid add-ons.
cards.goal: The client picks one name (or two to test) and sends it to legal clearance.

structure.does: Positioning in one line, audience, markets and languages, competitors' names, must-haves and no-gos the client gave.
3-4 directions (descriptive, suggestive, evocative or metaphor, coined, founder or place) with one line on what each says about the brand.

Each name with: why it fits, how to say it (simple respelling), meaning and connotation checks in the markets' languages (Hindi plus the regional language, English slang), length and spelling-from-hearing test.
For each finalist: exact-match domain (.com / .in) status, main social handles, and a preliminary trademark search note in the relevant classes, marked 'preliminary, needs attorney clearance'.
Top 2-3 with the reason and the risk of each, and what to test next (say-it-aloud test, quick audience poll).

length.note: Driven by the number of names and how many languages need meaning checks.

checklist: Does every name have a one-line rationale tied to the positioning?
Is each name spelled one obvious way when heard aloud (radio test)?
Has each name been checked for meanings and slang in Hindi, the target regional language and English?
Are domain, handle and trademark notes given for every finalist, and marked preliminary?
Do the names span at least three territories?
Is no finalist confusingly close to a competitor's name in the same category?
Is there a clear top recommendation with its risk stated?
pitfalls: Names that only work in English: test pronunciation and meaning in the regional languages the brand will sell in, and in Roman spelling on WhatsApp.
Saying 'trademark available' from a quick search. Write 'no identical mark seen in a preliminary search of class 30; needs attorney search'.
Clever spellings (Kwik, Xpress) that customers cannot type into search. Run the spell-from-hearing test.
A shortlist of near-synonyms from one territory. Spread across territories so the choice is real.
cards.exemplar_brief: Name shortlist for a Bengaluru millet-snack D2C startup selling baked millet chips to office-goers 25-40 on Swiggy Instamart and its own site; 10 names across 3 territories, each with rationale, respelling, Hindi and Kannada meaning check and preliminary domain/handle/trademark flags; English; 500-800 words; recommend the top 2.

verified.note: P2 S1 Sp2 V2 C2. Recap with positioning, competitors and no-gos; three territories; 10 names each with respelling, rationale and language checks that are correct and useful (siri paya in Hindi, navane/jola/tindi in Kannada, tinda, kodu = give); availability flags honestly marked as estimates needing searches and attorney clearance; top 2 with risk and a say-it-type-it test. Writer faults: Millet Byte has no Hindi/Kannada check; territory C is labelled 'coined' but holds real words (Tindi, Kodo, Ragaa); the top pick Four O'Clock has its own spell-from-hearing problem (4 O'Clock / Four Oclock) that the piece does not flag.

cards.name: Brand story / brand narrative
cards.summary: The founding story and point of view a brand tells the same way everywhere: About page, pitch deck, packaging, founder interviews. A good one is a true scene with a problem, a decision and proof, and it makes the customer, not the founder, the person the story is for.
use_for: About pages and 'Our story' sections
pitch-deck and investor narrative
founder interviews and PR backgrounders
a short version for packaging and marketplace brand stores
avoid: origin myths that are not true or cannot be shown: misleading in ads, and readers check
a founder biography with no customer in it: write genre:professional_bio for that
a manifesto of beliefs without events: use genre:brand_manifesto

sources.title: Fiverr: Brand Voice & Tone subcategory
sources.supports: 371 gigs on 2026-10-04; deliverable filter = Brand narrative, Mission & vision statement, Voice & tone guidelines, Target audience & positioning, Business name & slogan

sources.title: Upwork In-Demand Skills 2026 (2026-02-04)
sources.supports: top-10 most in-demand Sales & Marketing skills include Email Marketing, Marketing Automation, Lead Generation; fastest-growing include Brand Strategy (+26%) and Social Media Strategy (+36%)

cards.value_why: Fiverr's Brand Voice & Tone subcategory (371 gigs, 2026-10-04) lists Brand narrative as a deliverable; brand messaging rides on Brand Strategy, a fastest-growing Upwork skill in 2026 (+26%).
cards.goal: The reader trusts the brand enough to buy, follow or take the meeting, and can retell the story in one sentence.

structure.does: Opens on a specific scene: date or season, place, what the founder saw or lost. No 'since childhood I was passionate'.
What was wrong for people like the customer, in their words and with a concrete cost.
What the founders chose to do differently and what it cost them (a job, savings, a supplier relationship).
What exists now that shows the promise is kept: numbers, people, process, places.

structure.part: The customer's place and next step
structure.does: Where the brand is going, how the reader is part of it, and one action.

length.note: Deliver three cuts: full About-page story, a 50-80-word short version, and a one-sentence version. Video versions are timed to 60-90 seconds.

checklist: Does it open on a specific scene (time, place, event) rather than a general statement?
Is the customer's problem stated in concrete terms?
Is there a decision with a cost to the founders?
Is there at least one piece of proof a reader could check?
Is every fact in it true and approved by the client?
Does it end with the reader's role and one action?
Are the short and one-sentence versions consistent with the long one?
pitfalls: Stock origin lines ('humble beginnings', 'a dream to change the world'). Ask the founder for the day it started and write that day.
Founder as hero of every paragraph. Shift the light to the customer's problem and what changed for them.
Embellishing (grandmother's secret recipe that is not one). Interview the founder and keep to what can be shown.
Different versions of the story on the website, deck and Instagram. Lock the facts and the one-sentence version first.

ban.label: stock origin cliche
ban.regex: (?i)\b(humble beginnings|passion for excellence|since time immemorial|the rest is history|our journey began)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: About-page brand story for 'Sahyadri Sun', a Nashik family farm that sold raisins to mandi traders for 20 years and now sells sulphur-free raisins direct to urban health-conscious buyers; facts supplied: 2019 price crash at the Pimpalgaon mandi, 14 partner farms, residue tests on every batch; English; 400-600 words plus a 60-word short version; CTA to shop the trial pack.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Opens on a dated scene (spring 2019, father at the Pimpalgaon mandi, price named, drive home in silence), concrete customer problem (sulphur-treated gold raisins, no traceability), a decision with a real cost (traders refuse darker raisins, first season a fraction of volume), proof with the supplied facts (14 farms, residue test on every batch, batch on the pack), reader role and trial-pack CTA; 60-word and one-sentence versions match the long one. Price, test cost and lab are visible placeholders (not supplied). Nit: subheads 'What was wrong / What we decided / What exists now' read like the card's part names on a live About page; rename them.

cards.name: Brand voice & tone guide
cards.summary: A working document that defines how a brand sounds so any writer, agency or AI tool can produce on-brand copy: 3-4 voice traits with 'this, not that', tone shifts by situation, vocabulary to use and avoid, mechanics, and before/after rewrites. Good guides are used daily; weak ones are adjective lists nobody opens.
use_for: onboarding freelancers, agencies and support teams
the brand rules an AI writing tool or system prompt follows
aligning Hindi, Hinglish and English copy across channels
a rebrand or new market launch
avoid: a visual identity manual: logos and colours belong to the designer's brand book
voice traits with no examples: every trait needs a rewrite showing it
a 40-page PDF nobody reads: keep the core to what fits on a few screens and link the rest

sources.title: Fiverr: Brand Voice & Tone subcategory
sources.supports: 371 gigs on 2026-10-04; deliverable filter = Brand narrative, Mission & vision statement, Voice & tone guidelines, Target audience & positioning, Business name & slogan

sources.title: The Grey Hawks: Copywriting agency in India (service menu)
sources.supports: Indian agency menu leading with brand voice & messaging framework

sources.title: Mailchimp Content Style Guide: Voice and tone
sources.supports: widely used public example of a voice and tone guide with traits and situational tone

buyers: startups and D2C brands scaling content
cards.value_why: Fiverr lists 'Voice & tone guidelines' as a deliverable (371 gigs, 2026-10-04) and Indian agency menus lead with brand voice; demand grows as teams brief AI tools (trend:ai_assisted_writing_mainstream).
cards.goal: A new writer can produce copy the brand team approves on the first round.

structure.does: Who uses the guide, for which channels, who owns it and when it was last updated.
3-4 traits, each as 'X, not Y' (e.g. 'Direct, not blunt') with a one-line definition and a do/don't example.
How the voice flexes: celebration, error or outage, complaint, sales, legal, condolence. One sample line each.
Words we use, words we avoid (with the replacement), product terms with fixed spelling, competitor and sensitive terms.
Indian vs US English spelling, number and currency formats (Rs / ₹, lakh/crore), Hinglish rules (Roman or Devanagari, which English words stay English), emoji, exclamation and capitalisation policy.
Real off-brand copy rewritten on-brand, per channel (app, WhatsApp, Instagram, email), with a note on what changed.
Yes/no checks a writer runs before submitting.

length.note: Number of channels and languages drives length; keep the core under a few screens and put long word lists in an appendix.

checklist: Does each voice trait have a 'not' side that rules something out?
Does each trait have at least one do/don't example?
Does the tone section cover an error or complaint situation, not only happy ones?
Does the vocabulary list give a replacement for each banned word?
Are language rules explicit for every language the brand writes in (including Hinglish script choice)?
Are there at least five before/after rewrites taken from real channels?
Is there an owner and an update date?
pitfalls: Traits every brand claims (friendly, professional, innovative). Pair each with what it is not and show it in a rewrite.
No guidance for bad moments. Brands sound worst in outages and refunds; write those tone rules first.
Hinglish left to taste: writers mix scripts and spellings. Fix the script, the spelling of common words and which English terms stay English.
A guide written once and never tested. Give two writers the same brief using the guide; where their drafts differ, the guide is vague.
cards.exemplar_brief: Voice and tone guide for 'TokriNow', a Lucknow-based quick-commerce grocery app serving Hindi-belt cities; covers app microcopy, WhatsApp order updates and Instagram; English plus Hinglish (Roman) rules; 3 voice traits, 6 tone situations including a late delivery and a refund, a 20-row vocabulary table, 6 before/after rewrites; 1,000-1,500 words.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Owner/date/review cycle; three traits as 'X, not Y' with do/don't lines in natural Roman Hinglish ('Aapka order 20 min late hai. Hamari galti hai.'); six situations incl. late delivery, refund and an Instagram complaint, each with a sample; a 20-row use/avoid/why table with a replacement for every banned word and fixed product spellings; explicit mechanics (Rs vs the rupee sign, lakh/crore, Roman-only vs Devanagari, fixed Hinglish spellings, which English words stay English, emoji and exclamation policy); six channel-labelled before/after rewrites with what changed; an 8-item checklist. A new writer could ship first-round copy from this.

cards.name: Brochure / corporate collateral copy
cards.summary: Copy for a printed or PDF brochure, company profile, leaflet or leave-behind. Good brochure copy is written to the fold and the panel: a cover promise, benefit-led sections a skimmer can scan, proof, and a contact panel that makes the next step obvious.
use_for: company profile PDFs for SMEs, manufacturers and service firms
tri-fold leaflets for clinics, schools, real estate and events
trade-show and sales-meeting leave-behinds
services brochures emailed after a first call
avoid: a website pasted into panels: rewrite for the fold and the page
a full product range with specs: use genre:catalogue_copy
unproven superlatives ('India's leading'): in an ad these need substantiation under the ASCI code

sources.title: Elorites: Content Writing Services Prices 2026, India & USA (updated 2026-06-10)
sources.supports: India per-word rate tables by industry with separate rows for web pages, FAQ content, brochures and marketing material

sources.title: AWAI: 80 In-Demand Copywriting Projects (updated 2026-02-02)
sources.supports: copywriting pricing guide naming each project type with its own fee guideline

cards.value_why: Indian rate tables price brochures and marketing material as their own row (Elorites 2026) and AWAI lists multi-panel brochures as a project type; company profile PDFs are a common SME commission.
cards.goal: The reader contacts the company (call, WhatsApp, email, QR) or keeps the brochure for a decision.

structure.does: Who it is for and the main promise, plus brand name. A skimmer must know what is inside.
What the company does, for whom, and the one reason to choose it, with a proof point.
One section per service or product line: benefit headline, 2-4 lines of explanation, specifics (capacity, turnaround, certifications).
Named clients (with permission), numbers with time windows, certifications, a short testimonial.
Steps from enquiry to delivery, so the reader knows what happens after they call.
One clear action, phone, WhatsApp, email, address, QR to the right page.

length.note: A tri-fold leaflet has six panels and stays short; an 8-16-page company profile sits at the top of the range. Format and page count drive length; write to a word budget per panel.

checklist: Does the cover say who it is for and what they get?
Does every section headline state a benefit or outcome, not a department name?
Is each claim specific (number, time window, certification) rather than a superlative?
Does each panel or page fit its word budget?
Is there one primary action, with every contact detail correct?
Are client names and logos used with permission?
Is the copy readable by a non-native English buyer (short sentences, no idioms) when the brochure is for export?
pitfalls: History-first openings ('Established in 1987...'). Lead with what the buyer gets; put the year in the proof section.
'One-stop solution', 'state-of-the-art', 'best quality'. Replace with the machine, the capacity or the test result.
Too much text per panel. Write to a word budget per panel and cut to it.
Missing or buried contact. Put WhatsApp and phone on the back panel and the inside flap.
cards.exemplar_brief: Copy for an 8-page company profile PDF for 'Rajkot Precision Components' (demo name), a Rajkot CNC precision-parts manufacturer (ISO 9001:2015 certified, 42 machines, supplies auto and pump makers) seeking export buyers in the UAE and Germany; English (global plain English); 900-1,300 words with a word budget per page; CTA: request a quote by email (export@rajkotprecision.example) or WhatsApp (+91 90000 00000, demo). It resumed in February 2025 with one shared collections file each morning. Before quoting RBI's co-lending rules, the writer checks the current directions and their effective date. English; 800-1,100 words.

verified.note: P1 S2 Sp1 V2 C2. A BFSI editor in Oct 2026 would send it back to update; verify and revise. cards.name: Political campaign slogan
cards.summary: A short, chantable line that carries a candidate's, party's or movement's message: easy to shout at a rally, paint on a wall and repeat on WhatsApp. Good slogans name one promise or contrast in two beats, work in the voters' own language, and stay within election law.
use_for: election campaigns from ward to national level
issue movements and civic campaigns (clean river, safe roads)
rally chants, wall writing, posters, jingles and social handles' bio lines
student union and association elections
avoid: appeals to religion or caste for votes and attacks on a rival's private life: the Model Code of Conduct prohibits them

structure.does: One promise, demand or contrast in two beats, chantable (rhyme, alliteration or a call-and-response split). Names the candidate or symbol where useful.
Call-and-response or repeatable form for rallies (leader calls the first half, crowd answers the second).
Wall-writing version, social bio or hashtag version, and a local-dialect version (Bhojpuri, Awadhi, Maithili) where the constituency speaks it.
Which voter concern it answers, why the words were chosen, and the legal check done.

checklist: Can a crowd chant it in two beats after hearing it once?
Does it carry exactly one promise, demand or contrast?
Is it written in the voters' everyday language, with a dialect variant where relevant?
Is it free of any appeal to religion, caste or community for votes?
Is it free of personal attacks or unproven allegations against a rival?
Does the promise match the candidate's manifesto and record?

If it runs in paid electronic or social ads, is pre-certification planned with the right authority (ECI MCMC for Lok Sabha/Assembly polls; the State Election Commission's rules for municipal and panchayat polls)?
pitfalls: Literary Hindi that nobody says aloud. Use bolchaal words; test by asking three people from the constituency to repeat it.
Abuse or allegation as a slogan. It invites defamation and MCC complaints; attack the record with a checkable fact instead.
Two promises in one line (jobs and roads and water). Pick the one the constituency feels most and give the others their own lines.
Rhymes forced at the cost of meaning. If the rhyme bends the promise, drop the rhyme and keep the beat.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Headline has customer type, result and time window; snapshot readable alone; challenge with baselines turned into headcount (49 of 120 reps); one real obstacle (rural network, offline mode) told from the reps' side; results with baseline, after and period plus a qualitative change; honest data note (no control group); targeted demo CTA. Writer faults: the sales-head quote is drafted by the writer (flagged as draft, but it must come from the interview); the sales head is assumed male; prose is serviceable rather than memorable.

dealer and distributor price-list companions
trade-fair catalogues and B2B marketplace PDF uploads
product range sections inside a company profile

cards.name: CEO / founder letter
cards.summary: A letter in a leader's voice to customers, staff or shareholders about a milestone, a change or a crisis. A good one says the news in the first paragraph, explains what it means for this reader, takes ownership, lists concrete actions with dates, and sounds like the person who signs it.
use_for: price changes, policy changes and product shutdowns
milestones, funding announcements and anniversaries
crisis and outage letters to customers
annual-report chairman's or CEO's messages
letters to staff on restructuring or new direction
avoid: a press release in letter form: the press release (genre:press_release) is for media, the letter is for people the company owes
legal or regulatory disclosures: the company's lawyers and company secretary own those words
letters that hide the news in paragraph four: put it first

cards.goal: The reader understands the change, believes the leader, and stays (renews, stays subscribed, stays motivated, keeps holding).

structure.does: Addresses the actual group ('To everyone who orders from us', 'Dear shareholders'), not 'Dear valued customer'.
What is happening and when, in plain words, in the first 2-3 sentences.
The honest reason, with one specific fact (a cost, an incident, a number).
The concrete effect on this reader: price, access, timing, what they need to do (or not).
Actions with dates or numbers; in a crisis, ownership and an apology without excuses.
A human line in the leader's voice, a way to reply or reach a person, the leader's name and title.

length.note: Customer and staff letters stay short; annual-report messages run long because they cover the year's performance and outlook.

checklist: Is the news stated in the first three sentences?
Is the reason specific and honest, with one checkable fact?
Does it say exactly what changes for this reader and what they need to do?
Are actions given with dates or numbers?
In a crisis, does it take ownership without blaming customers, vendors or 'unforeseen circumstances'?
Does it sound like the signatory (checked against their past emails, talks or posts)?
Is there a way to reply or reach a person?
pitfalls: Corporate throat-clearing ('We are excited to share an update on our journey'). Start with the news.
Passive voice that hides who decided ('prices have been revised'). Write 'we are raising the price'.
Over-apologising without action, or acting without apologising. Do both, briefly.
A voice that is not the leader's. Read three things they wrote themselves and borrow their sentence length and words.
Data-breach letters drafted without counsel: under India's DPDP framework there are notice duties; check comp:dpdp_act_rules and the lawyer.

ban.label: corporate cliche

cards.exemplar_brief: Founder letter from Ananya Rao, co-founder of 'DabbaDay', a Bengaluru office-lunch subscription, to 9,000 subscribers announcing a price rise from Rs 3,999 to Rs 4,499 a month from 1 November; reasons supplied: vegetable costs up 18% this year and a move to steel tiffins; existing subscribers keep the old price for three months; English; 300-450 words; sent by email and linked from an app banner.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp1 V2 C2. Subject and first sentences state the news (Rs 3,999 to Rs 4,499 from 1 November); reasons named (vegetables up 18%, steel tiffins); exactly what changes (old price to 31 January, new from 1 February, nothing to do); actions with dates; candid founder voice ('I would rather tell you why than let you find it on a bill'); reply-to-me line. Writer fault: why the move to steel tiffins is left as a placeholder, though common sense supplies it (food stays hot, no plastic boxes), so the letter frames the tiffins only as a cost and never as a benefit to the subscriber.

cards.name: Character bio / character sheet
cards.summary: A working profile of one character that writers, actors or AI generators can build from: what they want, what they need, the wound behind it, how they talk, what they look like and how they change. Good bios describe behaviour and choices, not adjectives, and keep a fixed visual block that is reused word for word.
use_for: writers' rooms for series, micro-dramas, films and games
casting breakdowns for actors
AI video and image projects that need a consistent character across shots
brand mascots and recurring social characters
avoid: a backstory novel: keep only the history that drives present choices
trait lists ('kind, brave, complex') without behaviour: show each trait as something the character does
the story itself: use genre:film_treatment, genre:synopsis or genre:micro_drama_episode_script

cards.goal: Any writer, actor or AI shot prompt using the bio produces the same recognisable character.

structure.does: Name, age, role in the story and the core contradiction in one line.
External goal they chase, the internal need they resist, and the one past event that explains both.
What they do under pressure, habits, the flaw that causes trouble, shown as actions.
How they speak: language mix, pet phrases, sentence length, what they never say; 3 sample lines.
Age, build, face, hair, skin tone, wardrobe, colours, props, distinguishing marks, in one paragraph reused verbatim in every AI prompt.
Key people and what each wants from the character.
Who they are at the start and at the end, and the choice that turns them.

length.note: Leads get the full sheet; supporting characters a half-page. Number of relationships and episodes drives length.

checklist: Is the character's want stated as a concrete goal?
Is there a need or flaw that conflicts with the want?
Is every trait shown as a behaviour, not just named?
Are there sample dialogue lines that could only be this character?
Is the visual block specific enough to redraw (colours, clothes, marks) and written as one reusable paragraph?
Is the arc's turning choice named?
Does nothing in the backstory exist only for colour?
pitfalls: Adjective piles ('complex, multi-layered, larger than life'). Replace each with what the character does in a scene.
A visual description that changes between documents. Lock one block and paste it unchanged into every prompt and brief.
Dialogue samples that sound like the writer. Give the character one verbal habit and one thing they never say.
Wound as melodrama with no link to present choices. Keep the backstory event that explains today's behaviour; cut the rest.

ban.label: abstract trait label instead of behaviour
ban.regex: (?i)\b(a complex character|multi-layered|larger than life|has a heart of gold)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: Character bio for Guddu Mishra, 34, a Varanasi ghat boatman who becomes a reluctant YouTuber, lead of a 10-episode Hindi vertical micro-drama; for the writers' room and as the fixed visual block for AI shot generation; English bio with 3 sample dialogue lines in Hindi (Devanagari); 450-650 words.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Logline with contradiction; concrete want (own boat, notebook savings), need he resists, and a wound that explains present behaviour (father sold the boat, Guddu learned the price from the buyer); traits shown as actions (answers on the fourth ring, drops the fare to end an argument); a voice section with a habit and a never-says plus three in-character Devanagari lines; a reusable visual block specific enough to redraw; relationships with wants; arc with the episode-7 choice. Writer faults: who posts the viral clip is ambiguous (Pintu 'posts the first clip', Tara 'filmed the clip that spreads'); the Banarasi markers listed ('ई', 'का हो') never appear in the sample lines; the visual block runs ~110 words against 50-100.

bots that pretend to be human: say it is an assistant and offer a person
flows with no exit: every branch needs a 'talk to a person' path

Does every message ask for at most one thing?
Are common choices offered as buttons with short, front-loaded labels?
Does the bot confirm before booking, paying or cancelling?
Does every flow have a path to a person, with hours or wait time?
Do error messages say what went wrong and how to fix it?
If personal data is collected, does the bot say why and link the privacy notice?
Is there a language switch where users speak more than one language?

Open questions where buttons would do ('How can I help you today?' with no options). Offer the top 3 intents as buttons.
A bot that loops the same fallback. After two misses, offer a person.
Collecting phone, address or health data without saying why. Under DPDP, consent needs a clear notice; keep a one-line purpose and a link.
LLM bots with no scope rules. Write what it must refuse (medical diagnosis, prices it cannot confirm) and when it must escalate.

cards.name: Children's picture book text
cards.summary: A short read-aloud story told together with illustrations, written spread by spread for young children. Good picture-book text is lean, rhythmic and fun to read aloud, leaves the pictures to show what the words do not say, uses page turns for surprise, and lets the child character solve the problem.
use_for: trade picture books for ages 2-7
self-published KDP picture books
bilingual or Indian-setting stories for schools, NGOs and reading programmes
brand or festival storybooks for children
avoid: describing every illustration in the text: leave room for the art and add sparse art notes only where the text cannot work without them
a stated moral at the end: let the action carry the lesson
older readers' fiction: chapter books and middle grade need a different form (genre:short_story, genre:novel_chapter)

cards.goal: A parent or teacher reads it aloud and the child asks for it again.

structure.does: Introduces the child character and what they want or fear, in the first lines.
Something gets in the way; the stakes are child-sized and real (a lost kite, a scary sound).
The character tries and fails, each try bigger or funnier; a refrain repeats so the child can join in.
It looks hopeless, then the child finds the answer through their own action; a page turn delivers the surprise.
The problem is solved and the last line echoes the opening or the refrain with a twist.
Only where the picture must show something the text leaves out, in brackets.

length.note: A drafting range, not a publisher rule: confirm the target publisher's or series' word guidance before writing. Board books for toddlers run far shorter. Lay the text out spread by spread.

checklist: Is the text laid out spread by spread?
Does the child character want something by the end of the first spread?
Does the child solve the problem through their own action, not an adult's?
Is there a refrain or pattern a child can join in?
Is there at least one page-turn surprise?
Does the text avoid describing what the pictures will show (except sparse art notes)?
Does it read aloud smoothly with no tongue-twisters unless intended?
Is the ending free of a stated moral?
pitfalls: An adult fixes the problem. Let the child find the answer, even a small one.
Narrating the pictures ('Riya, who wore a red frock, stood under the big green tree'). Cut what the art will show; keep what only words can do.
The moral spelled out ('And so Riya learned that...'). End on action or the echo line.
Rhyme that forces odd words. Write in prose unless the rhyme and metre are perfect; read it aloud to check.

ban.label: stated moral
ban.regex: (?i)\b(the moral (of the story )?is|and (so )?(he|she|they) learned (that|to)|this teaches us)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: Picture-book text 'Mishti and the Thunder Drum' for ages 3-6: a girl in a Kolkata para is scared of monsoon thunder and finds her own way to stop being afraid; for a small Indian children's publisher; English with two or three Bengali words; 450-650 words laid out over 14 spreads with sparse art notes; includes a refrain and a page-turn reveal.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. 14 spreads, 512 words; want stated on spread 1 ('the rain, without the BOOM'); three escalating tries (hide, hum, shout) with the 'Gur-gur-gur... BOOM!' refrain to join in; the page-turn reveal from spread 6 to 7 (the thunder is a dhaak, the sky is practising); Mishti solves it herself with a pot and spoons ('Nobody helped her. Nobody had to.'); ending echoes the opening with a twist and no moral; one sparse, funny art note. Bengali words (para, Thakuma, dhaak) and Kolkata detail (tram bell, Howrah) sit naturally; reads aloud cleanly.

newsletters or offers to people who never opted in, in jurisdictions that require consent (check comp:uk_pecr, comp:dpdp_act_rules)
long pitches with attachments: the first email asks for interest, the deck comes after a reply

One low-friction, interest-based question ('Worth a 15-minute call next week?').
Real name, role, company, phone; for US recipients a postal address and an opt-out line.
2-3 short bumps, each adding something new (a useful link, a different angle, a referral ask), then a polite close-the-loop.

length.note: Body words of the first email, excluding signature. Shorter wins when the trigger is specific; follow-ups shorter still.

checklist: Does the first line mention something specific to this prospect that could not be sent to anyone else?
Is the email under 150 words in the body?
Is there exactly one ask, phrased as a question?
Is there one concrete proof point with a number and time window?
Is the subject line honest about the content (no fake 'Re:' or 'Fwd:')?
Is it plain text with no images, attachments or more than one link?
Does the signature carry a real name and, for US recipients, a postal address and opt-out?
Do follow-ups add new value instead of 'just bumping this up'?
pitfalls: Opening with yourself ('My name is... we are a leading...'). Open with their trigger; your name is in the signature.
Fake personalisation ('I loved your recent post!' with no detail). Name the post and what in it connects to your offer, or skip it.
Three asks (call, deck, referral). Pick one.
Deliverability ignored: a great email from an unauthenticated, cold domain lands in spam. See trend:email_deliverability_rules before scaling.
Deceptive subject lines and missing opt-outs break CAN-SPAM for US prospects. Keep the subject honest and the opt-out visible.
